body.text: A Queensland man who waited nearly three hours for an ambulance while "bleeding out" is calling on the health minister to "own the crisis" in the wake of the death of three people.
Carl Hartnett, 51, said he believed he nearly died waiting for help after slashing a major vein in his hand late at night on September 25, despite calling three times.
The Bribie Island veterinary nurse said he had tripped over a treadmill on his back deck in the dark, with a glass in his hand, which then smashed once he fell.
"It had cut quite deeply into my right hand, and I knew straight away I was in big trouble," he said. "I tried to grab a compress and stop the bleeding, but it would not stop."
His mother Sue Parker, who is 76 and could not drive him due to her own health issues, called Triple Zero (000). Mr Hartnett first spoke to an operator at 10:07pm.
Mr Hartnett said he did not panic because he was told help was on its way and that in the meantime someone would call to check on his condition.
But no-one came and the phone remained silent.
He said after about 90 minutes he started to question why he had not received an update.
"I am starting to feel a little bit dizzy, a little bit faint, I have probably lost about 800 to 900 mills of blood at this stage," he said. "The towel is starting to soak through."
At 11:29pm his mother called Triple Zero again.
Mr Hartnett then managed to speak to a different call centre operator but said he was hard to understand and was very rushed.
"It only lasted about two and a half minutes. He just did not ask the right questions," he said.
"I was told, 'you are on the system, we are coming to you, just hang on.'"
Mr Hartnett said the operator asked him whether the bleeding was under control.
"I do not know how they think I could tell the bleeding had totally stopped, I have a towel around it which is soaking in blood," he said.
"In the meantime I have laid down, stayed super calm, I knew they were coming."
At midnight, two hours after his mother first called, Mr Hartnett said he started hallucinating and had a full near-death experience.
"I think it is your body's way of getting you ready to no longer be here," he said.
By now Mr Hartnett had lost more than a litre of blood.
"I knew I was on the way out, my whole body, no energy, nothing left in the tank, I was totally drained, and I knew I was in big trouble," he said.
At 12:34am, he asked his mum to call Triple Zero again and told her, "I have about 10 to 15 minutes, I reckon".
"To the best of my memory, I told the operator that if they could not get an ambulance to me within 10 minutes, not to bother," Mr Hartnett said.
The Queensland Ambulance Service (QAS) categorised it as a Code One, which is used to indicate a potentially life-threatening event.

When paramedics arrived, Mr Hartnett said he was told his pulse was down to 40, his blood pressure through the floor, and he was suffering a bradycardia event — whereby the heart rate dramatically slows.
"They called in an intensive care paramedic and started IV fluids immediately. I believe they saved my life, and I have formally thanked them," he said.
"My concern is the system that left me waiting, not the frontline workers."
Mr Hartnett spent several days in the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital, where he underwent plastic and orthopaedic surgery.
He is grateful to be alive.
"I was determined to sort of give it a red hot go at living, so I was not giving up. It was really scary, it was the closest I have ever come."
Mr Hartnett came forward after hearing of the death of three people in Queensland while waiting for an ambulance in recent days.
This follows the death of Nick Bradford, who had a heart attack last month while waiting for help.
Mr Hartnett is calling on Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls to "own the crisis".
"Really step up and do something now before someone else dies because it is going to be on your shoulders."
He has also sent formal complaints to the Queensland Health Ombudsman and Queensland Ambulance Service (QAS) demanding answers.
In a statement, a QAS spokesperson said its clinical hub maintained contact with the patient and provided clinical oversight before paramedics arrived.

"We are working closely with hospitals to support the timely transfer of patients to emergency departments," the spokesperson said, adding that they wanted to thank Mr Hartnett "for the compliment he provided about the care he received and the professionalism of our paramedics".
The ABC has contacted the health minister for comment.
